handoff.summary: Batch b01 curates 4 atomic computer-science records: Amdahl fixed-workload speedup, transfer time D/R, storage capacity N*r, and two-component series availability product. All use directly inspected sources (Wikipedia Amdahl/Availability/RBD, Berkeley CS61C Amdahl notes, GeeksforGeeks transfer-time page, NIST binary-prefix page, Wikipedia data-rate/gigabyte pages, EventHelix series/parallel page, ReliaSoft/Ebeling reference page) accessed 2026-11-01. Statuses are requires-extension (new meanings). 11 reference cases and 6 rejection cases included.

assumptions: Source assumption: fixed workload W; f is the fraction of original (pre-enhancement) execution time affected by the enhancement, and s is the speedup factor applied to that affected part.
Application profile: deterministic bound ignoring parallel overhead, communication, synchronization and resource contention.
The unaffected fraction (1 - f) runs at original speed; the affected part runs s times faster.

gaps: Quantity meanings overall_speedup, parallel_fraction and component_speedup are absent from runtime-vocabulary.json; scalar form 1/((1-f)+f/s) fits the engine once meanings exist.
Unit 1 (dimensionless) needs an explicit integration-time decision.

models.inverse_notes: Solve directions: given S and s, f = (1 - 1/S)/(1 - 1/s) requires s != 1 and S != 0; given S and f (f != 1), s = f/((1/S) - (1 - f)) requires (1/S) > (1 - f). Boundaries: f=0 gives S=1 for any s (checked); f=1 gives S=s; as s -> infinity with f<1, S -> 1/(1-f). Substitution check: S=1.2, s=2 gives f=(1-1/1.2)/(1-1/2)=(1/6)/(1/2)=1/3, matching the Berkeley case. Zero/ambiguous: s=1 gives S=1 for all f (f underdetermined); s<=0 excluded by guard, not a scientific solve direction. Algebraic inversion does not establish causal invertibility of the workload split.
limitations: Excludes scaled-workload (Gustafson) interpretations where problem size grows with processor count.
Excludes overheads: communication, synchronization, load imbalance and non-constant s across the affected fraction.
f must be a time fraction of the original execution, not an instruction-count or code-size fraction; misidentifying f invalidates the bound.

references.method: Published worked example on the inspected Wikipedia Amdahl's law page: p=0.3, s=2 yields S=1/(0.7+0.15)=1/0.85=1.17647 reported as 1.18. Expected keeps the reported rounded value; tolerance 0.005 covers the rounding.
references.provenance: Published result from inspected source (Wikipedia Amdahl's law, Parallel programs section).

references.method: Published Berkeley CS61C worked example: one third of a program accelerated by 2 gives 1/(2/3+(1/3)/2)=1.2. Inputs use the closest binary64 to 1/3; expected keeps the reported 1.2 with tolerance covering float rounding.
references.provenance: Published result from inspected source (Berkeley CS61C parallel-performance notes, Amdahl examples section).

references.method: Limiting identity: with no improvable fraction the overall speedup is 1 regardless of s. Independent of the equation under test as a definitional boundary of the workload split.
references.provenance: Independent limiting identity (boundary check), not a source-reported measurement.

rejection_cases.reason: Parallel time-fraction above 1 violates the f <= 1 guard; a fraction of original time cannot exceed the whole.
Component speedup s is an asserted input, never inferred; omitting s leaves the bound undetermined.

relationship.locator: Definition section: overall-speedup display equation and parallel-programs worked example (S_latency = 1/(1-p+p/s)); derivation section defines p as the fraction of execution time benefiting and s as the acceleration factor.
relationship.translation_notes: Source symbols time_optimized (proportion of time) and speedup_optimized renamed to locals f and s; output Speedup_overall renamed to S. Dimensional check: all terms dimensionless (fraction divided by dimensionless factor), so S is dimensionless (unit 1). No unit conversion applied; pure arithmetic literals 1 only. Amdahl's 1967 AFIPS paper (DOI 10.1145/1465482.1465560, pp. 483-485) is cited as origin but the closed form is sourced here from the inspected pages, since the paper states the argument in prose.

assumptions: Source assumption: transfer rate R is the sustained (not peak/burst) average rate over the transfer, excluding cache/buffer benefit, per the inspected HDD-performance wording.
Application profile: ideal bulk-transfer bound; seek time, rotational latency, protocol overhead and contention are excluded and accounted by separate models.
Data size D and rate R use consistent data units (both bytes or both bits); bit/byte and decimal/binary conversions are separate models.

gaps: Quantity meanings data_size, transfer_rate and transfer_time are absent from runtime-vocabulary.json; scalar form D/R fits the engine once meanings exist.
Units B and B/s (or bit and bit/s) and the decimal/binary convention need explicit integration-time decisions.

models.inverse_notes: Solve directions: D = T*R requires T and R; R = D/T requires T != 0 plus the original guards (D>=0, R>0). Substitution check: T=8, R=125000000 gives D=1000000000, matching the gigabyte reference. Zero/ambiguous: D=0 gives T=0 for any positive R (degenerate empty transfer); T=0 with D>0 would require infinite R and is excluded by finite-rate guard. Inversion is algebraic only and does not turn a peak rate into a sustained rate.
limitations: Excludes disk access components (seek, rotational latency): transfer time is one component of access time, not total I/O time.
Excludes protocol/encoding overhead, retransmissions and shared-link contention unless included in the asserted sustained rate.
A peak or interface rate must not be substituted for the sustained rate; doing so underestimates time.

references.method: Independent arithmetic from two inspected unit facts: 1 GB = 10^9 B (NIST/IEC decimal) and 1 Gbit/s = 125,000,000 B/s (data-rate table). 10^9/125x10^6 = 8 s. Independence comes from combining unit definitions, not replaying a transfer-time example.
references.provenance: Independent derivation from published unit definitions in inspected sources.

assumptions: Source assumption: uniform record/object size r in the stated encoding, and a single stated decimal/binary unit convention (GB = 10^9 B vs GiB = 2^30 B per NIST/IEC 60027-2 and IEC 80000-13).
Application profile: raw capacity accounting; file-system metadata, spare/provisioned overhead, compression and deduplication are excluded.
Count N and size r refer to the same population of records and the same unit convention.

gaps: Quantity meanings record_count, record_size and storage_capacity are absent from runtime-vocabulary.json; scalar form N*r fits the engine once meanings exist.
Units for count (1 vs records) and data (B) and the decimal/binary convention need explicit integration-time decisions.

models.inverse_notes: Solve directions: N = C/r requires r != 0; r = C/N requires N != 0; both retain the original nonnegative guards. Substitution check: C=400000000000, r=1000000000 gives N=400, matching the 400-GB reference. Zero/ambiguous: r=0 forces C=0 for any N (degenerate zero-size records); N=0 gives C=0. Inversion is algebraic and does not recover per-record overhead or the unit convention.
limitations: Excludes file-system/directory metadata, RAID/parity overhead, spare provisioning, compression and deduplication.
A decimal/binary mix (e.g. GiB-sized records counted as GB) invalidates the result; the convention must be stated and consistent.
Non-uniform record sizes need summation, not this single-product form.

references.method: Independent arithmetic from the inspected gigabyte facts: 1 GB = 10^9 B and the worked 400 GB drive example (400 x 10^9 B). 400*10^9 = 4x10^11 B. Distinct from replaying the same equation because unit facts come from separate inspected pages.
references.provenance: Independent derivation from published unit definitions and the worked drive example.

assumptions: Source assumption: component up/down indicator variables are explicitly asserted to be mutually statistically independent at the evaluation instant (same steady-state mission/time and environment).
Application profile: binary repairable-component model; each Ai is the steady-state (limiting-average) availability, i.e. Pr[up], under stated conditions and ideal support unless otherwise qualified.
The two components form a series reliability block: the combination is up only if both parts are up.

gaps: Quantity meanings component_availability and series_availability are absent from runtime-vocabulary.json; scalar form A1*A2 fits the engine once meanings exist.
Unit 1 (probability) and the independence-assertion mechanism need explicit integration-time decisions.

models.inverse_notes: Solve directions: A1 = A/A2 requires A2 != 0; A2 = A/A1 requires A1 != 0; both retain the [0,1] guards and the independence precondition. Substitution check: A=0.989901, A2=0.9999 gives A1=0.99, matching the EventHelix pair. Zero/ambiguous: A=0 with A2>0 gives A1=0 (one failed component forces series failure); A2=0 leaves A1 underdetermined at A=0. Inversion is algebraic only and does not test independence.
limitations: Requires asserted independence; common-cause failures, shared repair/logistics contention or correlated environments invalidate the product (use dynamic RBD/Markov instead).
Excludes maintainability/logistics detail (spares, diagnostics, repair status) and k-out-of-N partial operation; this record is the two-component series closed form only.
Steady-state/limiting-average availability only; instantaneous or interval availability needs the time-dependent model.

references.method: Published EventHelix series table: X=99% (3.65 days/yr) with Y=99.99% (52 min/yr) combine to 98.99%. Expected keeps the reported 0.9899; tolerance 0.00005 covers display rounding of the exact product 0.989901.
references.provenance: Published result from inspected source (EventHelix series table).

references.method: Boundary identity: a series of perfect components is perfect under the definition. Independent limiting check.
Ordinary materially different case: a perfect component in series with a 0.5 component gives 0.5, showing the chain is bounded by its weakest link. Independent arithmetic.
references.provenance: Independent arithmetic check with synthetic inputs.

rejection_cases.reason: Availability above 1 violates the probability guard A1 <= 1; availabilities lie in [0,1].
Both component availabilities plus an explicit independence assertion are required; omitting A2 (or applying the product where independence was not asserted) is rejected per the RBD precondition.

relationship.locator: Availability page series-vs-parallel section: series formula and the 10-hosts-at-50% parallel corollary; RBD page: closed forms require statistical independence and series R_SYS = R1 x R2 x ...; EventHelix series section: A = Ax*Ay with the 99%/99.99% -> 98.99% table; ReliaSoft page: Ebeling (1997) Eq. 11.15 p.259 for n independent components in series.
relationship.original_equation: Availability of series component = (availability of component A) x (availability of component B) [x (availability of component C)]
relationship.translation_notes: Two-component restriction of the n-ary series product to fit the scalar format; locals A1, A2 and output A. Dimensional check: probability x probability = probability (dimensionless, unit 1). No conversion coefficients. Independence is a precondition recorded in assumptions, per the RBD page and Ebeling Eq. 11.15 naming.
